title: Void Ending in a Conjunction with Uranus
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The conjunction is the closest bond the Moon makes: at it, her strength takes on the nature of the planet she has joined, and the doctrine of the fifth quality treats her meeting with the Sun as the strongest of all her figures. A course that closes on a conjunction ends in union rather than separation, the Moon's virtue soaked through with the planet's own nature.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with a conjunction with Uranus, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his cold, sky-borne surprises. Uranus is nowhere in Picatrix: the planet was found with a telescope in 1781, some seven centuries after the book was written, and no passage of the source speaks of it. What follows is this almanac's extension of Picatrix's doctrine, never the medieval text's own words. Named for the Greek god of the sky, it is read here as a cold, far, sky-colored planet of upheaval, so that a course closing on it ends on a surprise rather than a settled end.
